title: Tasting Basics
description: Look, smell, taste: a simple order that lets you describe any wine and compare two of them.
L: Explain why a method helps you taste
Name the three steps of tasting
Set up good conditions for tasting

Drinking is enjoying. Tasting is noticing what you're enjoying, in an order that lets you compare. The method is simple: look, smell, taste. Doing it the same way each time builds a memory of wines you can draw on later.

Each step prepares the next. The look hints at age and body. The nose works before the palate because most of what we call flavour is smell: the tongue senses only sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami. When you sip, aromas travel up the back of the throat to the nose, a route called retronasal smell.
Why do you smell a wine before you taste it?
Most of what we call flavour is smell
The tongue registers five basic tastes. Everything else, from cherry to vanilla, is detected by smell, before and during the sip.

Taste in daylight or under white light, against a white background, with a clean, plain glass. Avoid perfume, coffee and toothpaste just before. Small changes like these make a bigger difference than expensive gear.
Put the steps of tasting in order.
Swirling releases aromas between looking and smelling. The conclusion comes once you've taken everything in.
A method turns drinking into tasting you can compare
Most flavour is smell, so the nose comes before the palate
White light, a plain glass and no strong smells help
Judge a wine's clarity and intensity
Explain what tears in the glass mean

Tilt the glass over a white surface. Check that the wine is clear, not hazy. Then judge intensity, from pale to deep, by looking at the core. Finally name the colour: lemon, gold or amber for whites; purple, ruby, garnet or tawny for reds.

Young reds look purple, because their pigments are fresh. With time, pigments bind with tannins and drop out, so the wine turns ruby, then garnet with an orange rim, and finally tawny. Whites go the other way: they deepen from pale lemon to gold and amber as they oxidise slowly.
Reds lose colour with age; whites gain it
A red wine has a garnet core and an orange-brown rim. What does this suggest?
Purple means youth. Garnet with an orange rim shows years of development, when pigments slowly change and drop out.

After swirling, drops called legs or tears run down the glass. They form because alcohol evaporates faster than water at the edge, changing surface tension. More and slower legs usually mean more alcohol or sugar. They tell you nothing about quality.
Legs show alcohol or sugar, not quality
Thick, slow legs on the glass show that a wine is of high quality.
Not true. Legs are physics: they come mostly from alcohol and sugar. A cheap, strong wine can have thicker legs than a great, lighter one.
Look for clarity, intensity and colour
Reds fade from purple to tawny; whites deepen to gold and amber
Legs show alcohol or sugar, never quality
Judge the intensity of a wine's aromas
Sort aromas into primary, secondary and tertiary
Smell in a way that finds more aromas

Before naming aromas, judge how strong they are: light, medium or pronounced. Then ask what they remind you of. A young Sauvignon Blanc jumps out of the glass; a young Chardonnay from a cool place may be much quieter. Neither is better, but it tells you about the grape and style.

Primary aromas come from the grape and fermentation: fruit, flowers, herbs. Secondary aromas come from winemaking: vanilla and toast from oak, butter from malolactic, bread from lees. Tertiary aromas come from age: leather, mushroom, honey, nuts, dried fruit. Naming the family tells you how the wine was made and how old it is.
Vanilla and toast in a wine usually come from:
Vanilla and toast are secondary aromas from oak barrels. Bottle age gives tertiary notes like leather and honey instead.

Swirl to lift aromas, then take short sniffs rather than one long one; your nose tires within seconds. Start with broad groups, like fruit or flowers, then narrow down: red fruit, then strawberry or cherry. Smelling real fruit, herbs and spices at home is the fastest way to build your vocabulary.
Which of these are tertiary aromas, from age?
Dried fruit, leather and mushroom develop with years in bottle or barrel. Fresh lime and green apple are primary fruit.
Primary aromas come from the grape, secondary from winemaking, tertiary from age
Short sniffs, broad to narrow, build skill fastest
Judge the length of the finish

On the palate you judge the wine's structure: sweetness, acidity, tannin, alcohol and body. Sweetness is felt on the tip of the tongue. Acidity makes your mouth water. Tannin dries your gums, like strong tea. Alcohol gives warmth at the back of the throat.

Tannins are compounds from skins, seeds and oak that bind to proteins in your saliva. That's why your mouth feels dry and rough. Acidity, mainly tartaric and malic acid in wine, triggers saliva, which is why acidic wines feel refreshing. Alcohol above about 14% starts to feel hot.
Tannin binds saliva; acid makes it flow
After a sip, your mouth waters for several seconds. Which element are you tasting?
Acidity triggers saliva. Tannin does the opposite, drying the mouth.

After you swallow or spit, notice how long the flavours last. A short finish fades in a few seconds. A long finish lingers for 10 seconds or more. Length is one of the clearest signs of quality, because only concentrated, well-balanced wines hold their flavour that long.
A wine that makes your gums feel dry and rough is high in ____.
Tannin binds to proteins in saliva, leaving that drying, gripping feel. Acidity would make your mouth water instead.
Sweetness, acidity, tannin, alcohol and body make up structure
Acid makes the mouth water; tannin dries it
A long finish is one of the clearest signs of quality
Write a short, useful tasting note
Compare two wines with the same words

A useful tasting note has four parts. Look: clarity, intensity, colour. Nose: intensity and main aromas. Palate: sweetness, acidity, tannin, alcohol, body, flavours, finish. Conclusion: is it good, and is it ready to drink? Short, specific words beat long poetic ones.

A wine is balanced when no element sticks out. Fruit should carry the acidity, tannin should be supported by fruit, alcohol shouldn't burn. Sweet wines need high acidity, or they feel cloying. A Sauternes can have 130 g/l of sugar and still feel fresh because its acidity is high.
A very sweet wine can feel balanced if its acidity is high enough.
Yes. Acidity cuts sugar, which is why great sweet wines feel fresh rather than syrupy.
Compare two wines side by side, using the same order and the same words. Differences that you'd miss in one glass become obvious next to another.
Which of these is the most useful line in a tasting note?
Lovely, a real joy to drink
Medium acidity, high tannin, blackcurrant and cedar, long finish
Tastes like a holiday in the sun
Specific words about structure and flavour let you, and anyone else, picture the wine and compare it.
A good note covers look, nose, palate and a conclusion
Balance means no single element sticks out
Comparing side by side with the same words sharpens your judgement
Taste a wine in a consistent order
Put the tasting steps in order.
Look, swirl to release aromas, smell, taste and only then conclude.
A white wine is deep gold. What is the most likely explanation?
It has some age or oak
Whites deepen in colour with age and time in oak. Very young, unoaked whites are pale lemon.
Aromas that come from age, like honey, leather and nuts, are called ____ aromas.
Primary aromas come from the grape, secondary from winemaking and tertiary from time.
Which are part of a wine's structure?
Structure is what you feel: sweetness, acidity, tannin, alcohol, body. Aromas and colour are separate parts of the note.
Legs on a glass are a reliable sign of quality.
Not true. They show alcohol and sugar, nothing about quality. Length of finish and balance tell you much more.
Look, smell, taste and conclude, every time
Colour tells age; aromas tell grape, winemaking and time
Structure is felt: acidity waters, tannin dries, alcohol warms
Balance and length are the clearest signs of quality
